text: The System Log application is built on one table, syslog, which captures platform log entries as the instance runs — scripts logging messages, the platform itself recording errors, and requests being tracked as they happen across the instance.

Every module under System Log is a filtered view over that table, the same way Properties pages are a filtered view over sys_properties, each one narrowing down to a specific kind of entry so you aren't scrolling through everything at once looking for one thing.

The real categories to know: System Log > All shows everything, unfiltered, useful when you don't yet know what you're looking for. Errors filters down to just error-level entries, usually where you start when something is visibly broken. Transactions shows web request-level logging, each record representing one individual request the instance processed. Script Log Statements shows messages scripts explicitly logged.

A script puts a message into the log with one of three real calls. gs.info for routine, informational messages confirming a script reached a certain point. gs.warn for something that isn't necessarily broken but deserves attention. And gs.error for an actual failure the script detected. The level the developer chose is your first signal for how seriously to treat any entry you find.

Back in Chapter 2's lesson on troubleshooting an access-denied issue, you learned to work through ACL evaluation logic by hand. The System Log is the tool that makes a much wider range of problems visible in the first place — not just ACL denials, but script failures, integration errors, and anything else logged.

The real workflow is simple and repeatable: reproduce the issue, note the exact time it happened, then check the relevant log view around that timestamp. A log can hold thousands of unrelated entries across the whole instance — without a timestamp to anchor your search, you're reading at random.
